image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Horizontal 100% stacked bar chart.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- **Stacking**: Each horizontal bar is divided into response categories that sum to 100%.  
- **Grouped rows / small-multiple-like categories**: Separate bars are shown for demographic/political groups (Overall, Men, Women, Democrats, Republicans, 18–34, 65+).  
- No faceting into separate panels.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Respondent group (Overall, Men, Women, Democrats, Republicans, 18–34, 65+) | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; row labels |
| Perceived seriousness response category (Not at all serious, Not very serious, Somewhat serious, Very serious) | Ordinal | Segment order within each stacked bar; color/hue |
| Percentage of respondents | Quantitative | Segment length/width along x-axis; text labels inside segments |
| Question topic: seriousness of not exercising freedom of speech due to fear of retaliation/harsh criticism | Categorical/nominal | Title/text annotation |

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that the overall population of the United States feels somewhat or very serious about the threat to free speech. I wonder if these statistics are due to an increase in cancel culture, or because of stricter government regulation. As both a woman and somewhat radical democrat, I feel increasingly worried about the ability of myself and others to express their criticism against the status quo, especially with the actions of recent administrations. One potential title could be: “Just How Free is American Speech? The Impact of Cancel Culture on Society.”

comments.raw_comment:
We noticed that the majority of the population surveyed believe it is somewhat to very serious in each group based on the percentages given in the graph. We wonder why more men believe retaliation or criticism for being able to use your first amendment right doesn’t matter as much as women believe it does. Another thing we are curious about is why adults aged 35-64 were not surveyed. The first thing that I noticed in this graph was that in general, most people think it is somewhat serious that some Americans do not exercise their freedom of speech due to fear. Within that, Democrats and Americans aged 18-34 are both the highest groups that believe this issue is somewhat serious. Conversely, Democrats have the lowest amount of individuals who think it is very serious. One thing that makes sense to me is that women were one of the highest groups of people who think it is somewhat serious and very serious. I think that this is due to a number of factors. Many women experience sexism & discrimination regularly in their everyday lives, and oftentimes probably hold back on what they really want to say in order to be safe. This is reinforced when you look at the male groups, who have the lowest numbers in both categories, which makes sense since they don't experience the same problems as women. Another thing that I noticed was that more Republicans believe that not exercising their freedom of speech out of fear was considered more serious than Democrats, even though the numbers are opposite for the somewhat serious category.

I wonder what the threshold is for something that is considered "very serious" versus "somewhat serious." Moreover, what are the demographics of race, ethnicity, and where they live? This dramatically affects the results.

This affects me and my community because I deserve to live my life being able to say what I want without criticism.

Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph shows responses to a national poll commissioned by the New York Times about what Americans think about problems we may now have with free speech and cancel culture.   This may have you ask:  How are free of speech and cancel culture related?

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response (and replies made to it) to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, April 29 with moderation on Wednesday, May 4.  The topic – hotter summer temperatures.  Keep noticing and wondering.

comments.raw_comment:
What's Going on in this Graph? - Free Speech

The four ratings for how much of a problem not exercising freedom of speech is are not at all serious, not very serious, somewhat serious, and very serious. The specific categories the responses are broken up into are men, women, democrats, republicans, ages 18-34, and ages 65+. Overall, 44% responded “somewhat serious” and 40% responded “very serious”. In all the categories “somewhat serious” or “very serious” are the largest response. 
I wonder why ages 35-64 are not included as an age category. There tends to be more interest in what younger people think versus what older people think, but what about all the people in between those age categories? I wonder if the categories men and women are referring to sex or gender, because if it is referring to gender there is another missing category of people. I wonder why Democrats is the category with the smallest percentage of “very serious”.
I would say that Americans being afraid to exercise freedom of speech in everyday situations is a somewhat serious problem. Politics and social issues are so contentious that probably everyone is afraid of saying something too controversial to their peers.
“Are people not using their freedom of speech?”
